A sphere-valued map cannot vanish outside a compact set. As approved by
the user on 2026-10-23, interpret spatial compact support as compact support
of a perturbation from a **fixed unit vector**, locally uniformly in time.
This is a disclosed nontrivial interpretation, not a claimed author-issued
correction.

Let \(n,m\geq1\) be integers and let
\(u:\mathbb R^n\times(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^m\) be jointly smooth.
Fix \(q\in\mathbb R^m\) with \(|q|=1\). Assume:

1. \(|u(x,t)|=1\) for all \(x\) and \(t>0\).
2. The acceleration \(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu\) is normal to the sphere at
   \(u\): at each point there is a real scalar \(a(x,t)\) with
   \(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu=a u\). No regularity of the selected scalar is
   assumed.
3. For every \(0<s<t<\infty\), a compact set
   \(C_{[s,t]}\subset\mathbb R^n\) exists such that \(u(x,r)=q\) for
   \(x\notin C_{[s,t]}\), \(r\in[s,t]\).

With Euclidean norms and Lebesgue measure, define

\[
e(x,t)=|u_t(x,t)|^2+\sum_{j=1}^n|\partial_{x_j}u(x,t)|^2,
\qquad E(t)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}e(x,t)\,dx.
\]

The spatial gradient square is the Frobenius square, and
\(\Delta_xu=\sum_j\partial_{x_jx_j}u\) component by component.
Prove integrability of \(e(\cdot,t)\), differentiability of \(E\),
and \(E'(t)=0\) for every \(t>0\). No assertion at time zero is required.
value.conclusion: For every t>0, the density e(·,t) is Lebesgue integrable on R^n, E is differentiable at t, and E'(t)=0. In particular E(t)=E(s) for all s,t>0. The density is |u_t|^2+sum_{j=1}^n|∂_{x_j}u|^2 with Euclidean norms, and E(t) is its spatial Lebesgue integral, with no factor 1/2. No assertion at time zero is made.

definitions.definition: For x in R^n and t>0, Δ_xu(x,t)=sum_{j=1}^n ∂_{x_jx_j}u(x,t), component by component. The notation u_t,u_tt,∂_{x_j}u and ∂_{x_j}u_t denotes the corresponding classical partial derivatives on R^n×(0,∞). D_xu is the m-by-n matrix with columns ∂_{x_j}u, and |D_xu|^2 is its Frobenius square sum_{j=1}^n |∂_{x_j}u|^2. Vectors have the Euclidean dot product and norm. Spatial integrals are Lebesgue integrals on R^n; boxes carry the restricted Lebesgue measure. int denotes topological interior and 1_A denotes the indicator of a set A.
e(x,t)=|u_t(x,t)|^2+sum_{j=1}^n |∂_{x_j}u(x,t)|^2, for x in R^n and t>0, with exactly the Euclidean and Frobenius normalization of problem.md:38-46.
For every t>0, E(t)=∫_{R^n} e(x,t) dx. This is the ordinary finite Lebesgue integral, used after spatial integrability has been established; there is no factor 1/2.

source_steps.text: Fix arbitrary x∈R^n and t>0. By H004 the identity u(x,r)·u(x,r)=1 holds for every r>0. H002 permits differentiating this scalar identity in r at t. The ordinary product rule for the finite Euclidean dot product gives 2u(x,t)·u_t(x,t)=0, hence u·u_t=0 at (x,t).

Choose a real scalar a at (x,t) from H005, so u_tt-Δ_xu=a u. Dot with u_t and use F001 and symmetry of the dot product: u_t·(u_tt-Δ_xu)=a(u_t·u)=0. This uses only a pointwise choice; no derivative or continuity of a is required.

Retain also the supplied explicit-equation calculation. Twice differentiating u·u=1 in time, using H002 and H004, gives 2|u_t|^2+2u·u_tt=0. Twice differentiating the same identity in each spatial coordinate gives 2|∂_{x_j}u|^2+2u·∂_{x_jx_j}u=0 for every j=1,...,n. Thus u·u_tt=-|u_t|^2 and u·∂_{x_jx_j}u=-|∂_{x_j}u|^2. Dot the chosen normality equation with u. Since u·u=1, a=u·(u_tt-Δ_xu)=sum_{j=1}^n|∂_{x_j}u|^2-|u_t|^2. This computation applies to every scalar satisfying that equation at (x,t); substitute it back to obtain the explicit equation in the exported conclusion. Together with F001 and F002 these are all clauses of the exported conclusion. The point (x,t) was arbitrary, and the scalar witness's private identity does not occur in the resulting equation, so quantify over all x and t>0.
Fix t0>0 and put J=[t0/2,3t0/2]. Then 0<t0/2<3t0/2<∞. Instantiate H006 with these endpoints and choose its compact C. Thus u(x,r)=q for every x outside C and every r∈J.

A compact subset of finite-dimensional Euclidean space is bounded: the open boxes (-k,k)^n for positive integers k cover R^n and form an increasing family; compactness gives a finite subcover of C and therefore one containing box. For C empty any positive radius works. Consequently there exists R>0 with C⊂(-R,R)^n. This also exhibits the needed room between C and the boundary of the closed box.

Choose R>0 from F002 and set Q=[-R,R]^n. H001 ensures a finite positive number n of spatial coordinates. Q is compact and has Lebesgue measure (2R)^n<∞ by the rectangle formula. Since compact C is closed, (R^n\C)×int J is open. On that open set F001 says u is identically q. By H002 and locality of classical differentiation, every positive-order derivative of u is zero there: each component's difference quotients of a constant vanish, and this repeats for higher derivatives. Thus e,e_t and every derivative product listed in the exported conclusion vanish outside C at interior times.

Smoothness H002 makes e,e_t, u_t·u_tt, and, for each j=1,...,n, u_t·∂_{x_j}u, ∂_{x_j}u_t·∂_{x_j}u, u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u and ∂_{x_j}(u_t·∂_{x_j}u) continuous on R^n×(0,∞). At any fixed r∈int J, each is continuous and hence Borel measurable as a function of space. Its absolute value attains a finite bound on compact Q, and it is zero outside C by F003. Thus its absolute integral on R^n is at most its finite bound times |Q|=(2R)^n, proving integrability. These conclusions hold for every r∈int J and each spatial index. In particular t0∈int J, so e(·,t0) is integrable. Since t0 was arbitrary, e(·,t) is integrable for every t>0. The witnesses C,R and their definitions J,Q establish exactly the existential window assertion of the exported conclusion; none escapes as a globally fixed choice.

Fix t0>0. The scalar product rule and equality of mixed partial derivatives, valid because H002 is joint smoothness on the open space-time domain, give for every x∈R^n and r>0: e_t(x,r)=2u_t(x,r)·u_tt(x,r)+2sum_{j=1}^n∂_{x_j}u(x,r)·∂_{x_j}u_t(x,r). In particular e_t is continuous on that domain.

Set J=[t0/2,3t0/2], choose the compatible C and R>0 furnished by N002, and set Q=[-R,R]^n. For every r∈int J, e(·,r), e_t(·,r) and the terms in F001 are continuous and integrable, and vanish outside C⊂int Q. In particular E(t0) and the nearby energy integrals are finite by N002 and D003.

Choose eta=t0/4. Then [t0-eta,t0+eta]=[3t0/4,5t0/4]⊂int J. The continuous function |e_t| from F001 is bounded on the compact set Q×[t0-eta,t0+eta]; the extreme value theorem supplies a finite nonnegative bound. Thus there exists B≥0 such that |e_t(x,r)|≤B for every x∈Q and r∈[t0-eta,t0+eta].

Choose such B from F003. Define the total function v(h,x)=(e(x,t0+h)-e(x,t0))/h when 0<|h|<eta, and v(h,x)=0 otherwise. The density is evaluated only at positive times in the first branch. Define bnd(x)=B 1_Q(x). Q is a measurable box of finite measure by F002; hence bnd is integrable and its absolute integral is B|Q|<∞. For every 0<|h|<eta, H002 makes the two densities in v continuous in x; their scalar difference quotient is continuous and therefore strongly measurable as a real-valued function.

Fix arbitrary h∈R and x∈R^n. Temporarily assume L1: 0<|h|<eta. For x∈Q, apply M004 to the one-variable function r↦e(x,r) on the interval with endpoints min(t0,t0+h), max(t0,t0+h), and derivative r↦e_t(x,r). For purposes of the source's global domain R, extend both by zero at nonpositive times; the entire closed interval lies in (0,∞), where H002 and F001 give continuity and the asserted derivatives. The endpoints are distinct by L1. The source gives the difference quotient as e_t at an intervening time (the quotient is the same for either sign of h). By F003 its absolute value is at most B. For x∉Q, both densities vanish by F002, so the quotient is zero. The cases together prove |v(h,x)|≤B1_Q(x)=bnd(x). Discharge L1 and quantify over x and h to obtain: for all 0<|h|<eta and all x∈R^n, |v(h,x)|≤bnd(x).

Let ell be the punctured-neighborhood filter at 0 in R. It is countably generated: the punctured intervals 0<|h|<1/k for positive integers k form a countable base. F004 gives strong measurability of v(h,·) for all sufficiently small nonzero h, and integrability of bnd. F005 gives domination everywhere in x for those h. For each x∈R^n, differentiability in time from H002 and F001 gives v(h,x)→e_t(x,t0) along ell. Instantiate M001 with X=R^n and Lebesgue measure, V=R, I=R, this ell, F(h)=v(h,·), f(x)=e_t(x,t0), and bound bnd. All these conditions hold pointwise or eventually as required, so ∫v(h,x)dx→∫e_t(x,t0)dx as h→0, h≠0.

For 0<|h|<eta, F002 ensures that both densities in v are integrable. By linearity of the Lebesgue integral and D003, ∫v(h,x)dx=(E(t0+h)-E(t0))/h. Thus F006 proves differentiability of the actual finite function E at t0, with E'(t0)=∫e_t(x,t0)dx. Substitute F001 and use the integrability of all its terms from F002 and linearity over the finite spatial sum: E'(t0)=2∫u_t·u_tt dx+2sum_{j=1}^n∫∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t dx. All integrands are evaluated at t0. The choices were available for arbitrary t0>0, so universal introduction proves every clause of the exported conclusion.

Fix t0>0 and a spatial index j∈{1,...,n}. H001 gives n≥1, so the remaining-coordinate space has dimension n-1≥0. Set J=[t0/2,3t0/2], choose C and R>0 from N002, and put Q=[-R,R]^n. Since t0∈int J, N002 gives integrability of the derivative products in the exported conclusion and of ∂_{x_j}(u_t·∂_{x_j}u), all zero outside C. Also C⊂int Q and Q has finite measure.

Define g(x)=u_t(x,t0)·∂_{x_j}u(x,t0). By H002 it is smooth in x, and the product rule gives ∂_{x_j}g=∂_{x_j}u_t·∂_{x_j}u+u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u. It is zero off C by N002. As C is closed and contained in int Q, g is identically zero on the open complement of C, which contains the boundary of Q. Hence g vanishes on a neighborhood of that boundary. Define the coordinate insertion map Phi(y,s) by placing s in coordinate j and the vector y in the remaining coordinates, in increasing coordinate order.

Fix arbitrary y∈R^(n-1) and define phi(s)=g(Phi(y,s)) for s∈R. F002 and the chain rule give the derivative phi'(s)=∂_{x_j}g(Phi(y,s)) at every real s, including ±R. This derivative is continuous and hence bounded and Lebesgue interval-integrable on [-R,R]. Apply M003 with V=R, endpoints -R,R, f=phi, and derivative d(s)=∂_{x_j}g(Phi(y,s)). The integral equals phi(R)-phi(-R). Each endpoint has j-th coordinate ±R and is outside C⊂(-R,R)^n, so both values are zero by F002. Therefore ∫_{-R}^R ∂_{x_j}g(Phi(y,s))ds=0. Quantify over the arbitrary y. The oriented interval integral is the usual restricted Lebesgue integral here since -R<R, and including or deleting the singleton endpoints does not affect a Lebesgue integral.

Let Qother=[-R,R]^(n-1) and w(y,s)=∂_{x_j}g(Phi(y,s)). Splitting off coordinate j identifies Q with Qother×[-R,R]. Under Phi, Lebesgue measure on R^n is the product of Lebesgue measures on the remaining coordinates and on R: on every coordinate rectangle the image has exactly the product of the side lengths, and these rectangles generate the Borel sigma algebra; uniqueness of sigma-finite measures gives the identification, also for the completed Lebesgue integrals of the continuous functions used here. If n=1, the remaining-coordinate space is R^0, a singleton of measure 1, so the same statement holds. On the compact product box, w is continuous and bounded by F002, hence measurable and absolutely integrable. Its two summands from F002 have the same property, in agreement with F001. Apply M002 with X=R^(n-1), Y=R, V=R, the Lebesgue measures restricted to Qother and [-R,R], and f=w. These measures are finite, thus s-finite. The result and F003 yield ∫_Q∂_{x_j}g dx=∫_{Qother}(∫_{[-R,R]}w(y,s)ds)dy=∫_{Qother}0dy=0.

By F001 the derivative and both summands in F002 are zero outside Q, so their Q-integrals equal their R^n-integrals. Integrate the product rule F002, use F004 and linearity for the integrable summands from F001: 0=∫_{R^n}∂_{x_j}u_t·∂_{x_j}u dx+∫_{R^n}u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u dx, all at time t0. Symmetry of the dot product and rearrangement prove ∫∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t dx=-∫u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u dx. The asserted integrability is part of F001. Since t0 and j were arbitrary this proves the exported conclusion.

Fix arbitrary t0>0. N002 supplies integrability of e(·,t0) and all derivative products below, and legitimizes the energy definition D003. N003 gives E'(t0)=2∫_{R^n}u_t·u_tt dx+2sum_{j=1}^n∫_{R^n}∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t dx. Use N004 for each spatial index to obtain E'(t0)=2∫u_t·u_tt dx-2sum_{j=1}^n∫u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u dx. Linearity for this finite sum and D001 give E'(t0)=2∫_{R^n}u_t·(u_tt-Δ_xu)dx, with all integrands evaluated at t0. N001 says the last integrand is identically zero, hence E'(t0)=0.
The positive time t0 was arbitrary. By F001, for every r>0, e(·,r) is integrable and E is differentiable at r with E'(r)=0. This proves all requested analytic assertions, with no assertion at zero.

For completeness retain the supplied final conservation statement. Fix arbitrary s,t>0 and use the exhaustive order cases s=t, s<t, or t<s. In the equality branch introduce L3: s=t; substitution gives E(t)=E(s), and discharge L3. In the increasing branch introduce L1: s<t. F002 gives differentiability on (s,t) with derivative zero, and continuity on [s,t], since E is differentiable at every positive time, including the endpoints. Apply M004 to E extended by zero at nonpositive arguments, derivative function identically zero, and endpoints s,t. It gives 0=(E(t)-E(s))/(t-s), hence E(t)=E(s), since t-s>0. Discharge L1. In the decreasing branch introduce L2: t<s. Apply M004 with endpoints t,s and the same functions; it gives 0=(E(s)-E(t))/(s-t), hence E(t)=E(s), since s-t>0. Discharge L2. Each interval lies strictly in (0,∞), so the extension does not affect any value or derivative there. Case elimination gives E(t)=E(s) in all cases; quantifying over s,t proves constancy on (0,∞). Combining this with F002 proves the exported conclusion, with exactly the original density and normalization.

1: # Conservation of energy for a sphere-valued wave map
2: 
3: ## Original exercise
4: 
5: Lawrence C. Evans, *Partial Differential Equations*, second edition,
6: Graduate Studies in Mathematics 19, AMS, 2010, section 12.6, exercise 14,
7: printed page 694. The preceding exercise 13 defines the sphere-valued
8: wave map. ISBN: 978-0-8218-4974-3.
9: 
10: > 14. Prove that if \(\mathbf u\) is a wave map into the unit sphere,
11: > with compact support in space, we have conservation of energy:
12: > \[
13: > \frac{d}{dt}\int_{\mathbb R^n}
14: >       |\mathbf u_t|^2+|D\mathbf u|^2\,dx=0.
15: > \]
16: 
17: ## Fixed interpretation and complete target
18: 
19: A sphere-valued map cannot vanish outside a compact set. As approved by
20: the user on 2026-10-23, interpret spatial compact support as compact support
21: of a perturbation from a **fixed unit vector**, locally uniformly in time.
22: This is a disclosed nontrivial interpretation, not a claimed author-issued
23: correction.
24: 
25: Let \(n,m\geq1\) be integers and let
26: \(u:\mathbb R^n\times(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^m\) be jointly smooth.
27: Fix \(q\in\mathbb R^m\) with \(|q|=1\). Assume:
28: 
29: 1. \(|u(x,t)|=1\) for all \(x\) and \(t>0\).
30: 2. The acceleration \(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu\) is normal to the sphere at
31:    \(u\): at each point there is a real scalar \(a(x,t)\) with
32:    \(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu=a u\). No regularity of the selected scalar is
33:    assumed.
34: 3. For every \(0<s<t<\infty\), a compact set
35:    \(C_{[s,t]}\subset\mathbb R^n\) exists such that \(u(x,r)=q\) for
36:    \(x\notin C_{[s,t]}\), \(r\in[s,t]\).
37: 
38: With Euclidean norms and Lebesgue measure, define
39: 
40: \[
41: e(x,t)=|u_t(x,t)|^2+\sum_{j=1}^n|\partial_{x_j}u(x,t)|^2,
42: \qquad E(t)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}e(x,t)\,dx.
43: \]
44: 
45: The spatial gradient square is the Frobenius square, and
46: \(\Delta_xu=\sum_j\partial_{x_jx_j}u\) component by component.
47: Prove integrability of \(e(\cdot,t)\), differentiability of \(E\),
48: and \(E'(t)=0\) for every \(t>0\). No assertion at time zero is required.
49: 
50: ## Fixed natural-language proof
51: 
52: ### 1. Tangency and the wave-map equation
53: 
54: Differentiate \(u\cdot u=1\) in time. The product rule gives
55: \(2u\cdot u_t=0\), so
56: 
57: \[
58: u\cdot u_t=0,\qquad
59: u_t\cdot(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu)=a(u_t\cdot u)=0.          \tag{1}
60: \]
61: 
62: No derivative of \(a\) is needed. The familiar explicit equation also
63: follows from the assumptions: twice differentiating the unit constraint
64: gives \(u\cdot u_{tt}=-|u_t|^2\) and
65: \(u\cdot\partial_{x_jx_j}u=-|\partial_{x_j}u|^2\).
66: Dotting the normality equation with \(u\), using \(|u|^2=1\), yields
67: \(a=\sum_j|\partial_{x_j}u|^2-|u_t|^2\). This is a consequence,
68: not an additional PDE assumption.
69: 
70: ### 2. Common compact support and integrability
71: 
72: Fix \(t_0>0\), put \(J=[t_0/2,3t_0/2]\), and choose its compact
73: spatial set \(C\) from assumption 3. Since \(C\) is bounded, choose
74: \(R>0\) with \(C\subset(-R,R)^n\) and set \(Q=[-R,R]^n\).
75: The box has finite Lebesgue measure \((2R)^n\).
76: 
77: On the open set \((\mathbb R^n\setminus C)\times\operatorname{int}J\),
78: the map equals the constant \(q\), so all its positive-order
79: derivatives vanish. At interior times, \(e\), \(e_t\), and the
80: derivative products used below consequently vanish outside \(C\).
81: They are continuous by smoothness; their spatial sections are measurable,
82: bounded on \(Q\), and supported there. Their absolute integrals are
83: bounded by a finite constant times \(|Q|\). This proves integrability
84: of \(e(\cdot,t_0)\) and of all later terms. Since \(t_0\) was arbitrary,
85: the energy is a finite, well-defined integral at every positive time.
86: 
87: ### 3. Differentiate the energy integral
88: 
89: The product rule and equality of mixed derivatives give
90: 
91: \[
92: e_t=2u_t\cdot u_{tt}
93:    +2\sum_{j=1}^n\partial_{x_j}u\cdot\partial_{x_j}u_t.           \tag{2}
94: \]
95: 
96: Choose \(\eta>0\) so that
97: \([t_0-\eta,t_0+\eta]\subset\operatorname{int}J\).
98: Continuity of (2) on the compact box
99: \(Q\times[t_0-\eta,t_0+\eta]\) gives a finite bound \(|e_t|\leq B\).
100: For \(0<|h|<\eta\), the one-variable mean value theorem at fixed
101: \(x\) therefore gives
102: 
103: \[
104: \left|\frac{e(x,t_0+h)-e(x,t_0)}h\right|
105: \leq B\mathbf1_Q(x).
106: \]
107: 
108: Outside \(Q\), both densities vanish, so the bound holds throughout
109: \(\mathbb R^n\). The right side is integrable. The difference
110: quotients converge pointwise to \(e_t(x,t_0)\). Dominated convergence
111: and linearity for these integrable functions now prove
112: 
113: \[
114: E'(t_0)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}e_t(x,t_0)\,dx.            \tag{3}
115: \]
116: 
117: This establishes differentiability of the actual finite integral.
118: 
119: ### 4. Integration by parts and cancellation
120: 
121: For each spatial index \(j\), at time \(t_0\) put
122: \(g_j(x)=u_t(x,t_0)\cdot\partial_{x_j}u(x,t_0)\).
123: It is smooth and vanishes on a neighborhood of the boundary of \(Q\),
124: because \(C\subset\operatorname{int}Q\). The product rule gives
125: 
126: \[
127: \partial_{x_j}g_j
128: =\partial_{x_j}u_t\cdot\partial_{x_j}u
129:  +u_t\cdot\partial_{x_jx_j}u.
130: \]
131: 
132: Integrate first over \(x_j\in[-R,R]\) at fixed remaining coordinates.
133: The fundamental theorem of calculus gives zero because both endpoint
134: values of \(g_j\) are zero. Fubini applies on \(Q\) because the
135: derivative and its two summands are continuous and bounded on a
136: finite-measure box. Thus \(\int_Q\partial_{x_j}g_j=0\).
137: All these terms vanish outside \(Q\), so
138: 
139: \[
140: \int_{\mathbb R^n}\partial_{x_j}u\cdot\partial_{x_j}u_t\,dx
141: =-\int_{\mathbb R^n}u_t\cdot\partial_{x_jx_j}u\,dx.              \tag{4}
142: \]
143: 
144: Every integral is finite by step 2. Sum (4) over the finitely many
145: spatial indices and substitute (2) into (3):
146: 
147: \[
148: \begin{aligned}
149: E'(t_0)
150: &=2\int_{\mathbb R^n}u_t\cdot u_{tt}\,dx
151:  -2\sum_{j=1}^n\int_{\mathbb R^n}u_t\cdot\partial_{x_jx_j}u\,dx\\
152: &=2\int_{\mathbb R^n}u_t\cdot(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu)\,dx=0,
153: \end{aligned}
154: \]
155: 
156: by (1). This holds at every \(t_0>0\). Hence \(E\) is differentiable
157: with zero derivative on \((0,\infty)\), and is constant there by the
158: mean value theorem. This is conservation of energy with exactly the
159: normalization in the exercise.

32: We prove basic properties of these notions.
33: 
34: ## Main definitions and results
35: Let `f : E → F` be a map between normed vector spaces over a nontrivially normed field `𝕜`.
36: 
37: * `ContDiff 𝕜 n f`: expresses that `f` is `C^n`, i.e., it admits a Taylor series up to
38:   rank `n`.
39: * `ContDiffOn 𝕜 n f s`: expresses that `f` is `C^n` in `s`.
40: * `ContDiffAt 𝕜 n f x`: expresses that `f` is `C^n` around `x`.
41: * `ContDiffWithinAt 𝕜 n f s x`: expresses that `f` is `C^n` around `x` within the set `s`.
42: 
43: In sets of unique differentiability, `ContDiffOn 𝕜 n f s` can be expressed in terms of the
44: properties of `iteratedFDerivWithin 𝕜 m f s` for `m ≤ n`. In the whole space,
45: `ContDiff 𝕜 n f` can be expressed in terms of the properties of `iteratedFDeriv 𝕜 m f`
46: for `m ≤ n`.
47: 
48: ## Implementation notes
49: 
50: The definitions in this file are designed to work on any field `𝕜`. They are sometimes slightly more
51: complicated than the naive definitions one would guess from the intuition over the real or complex
52: numbers, but they are designed to circumvent the lack of gluing properties and partitions of unity
53: in general. In the usual situations, they coincide with the usual definitions.
54: 
55: ### Definition of `C^n` functions in domains
56: 
57: One could define `C^n` functions in a domain `s` by fixing an arbitrary choice of derivatives (this
58: is what we do with `iteratedFDerivWithin`) and requiring that all these derivatives up to `n` are
59: continuous. If the derivative is not unique, this could lead to strange behavior like two `C^n`
60: functions `f` and `g` on `s` whose sum is not `C^n`. A better definition is thus to say that a
61: function is `C^n` inside `s` if it admits a sequence of derivatives up to `n` inside `s`.
62: 
63: This definition still has the problem that a function which is locally `C^n` would not need to
64: be `C^n`, as different choices of sequences of derivatives around different points might possibly
65: not be glued together to give a globally defined sequence of derivatives. (Note that this issue
66: cannot happen over the real numbers, thanks to partitions of unity, but the behavior over a general
67: field is not so clear, and we want a definition for general fields). Also, there are locality
68: problems for the order parameter: one could image a function which, for each `n`, has a nice
69: sequence of derivatives up to order `n`, but they do not coincide for varying `n` and can therefore
70: not be glued to give rise to an infinite sequence of derivatives. This would give a function
71: which is `C^n` for all `n`, but not `C^∞`. We solve this issue by putting locality conditions
72: in space and order in our definition of `ContDiffWithinAt` and `ContDiffOn`.
73: The resulting definition is slightly more complicated to work with (in fact not so much), but it
74: gives rise to completely satisfactory theorems.
75: 
76: For instance, with this definition, a real function which is `C^m` (but not better) on `(-1/m, 1/m)`
77: for each natural `m` is by definition `C^∞` at `0`.
78: 
79: There is another issue with the definition of `ContDiffWithinAt 𝕜 n f s x`. We can
80: require the existence and good behavior of derivatives up to order `n` on a neighborhood of `x`
81: within `s`. However, this does not imply continuity or differentiability within `s` of the function
82: at `x` when `x` does not belong to `s`. Therefore, we require such existence and good behavior on
83: a neighborhood of `x` within `s ∪ {x}` (which appears as `insert x s` in this file).
84: 
85: ## Notation
86: 
87: We use the notation `E [×n]→L[𝕜] F` for the space of continuous multilinear maps on `E^n` with
88: values in `F`. This is the space in which the `n`-th derivative of a function from `E` to `F` lives.

3: Apply these requirements within the accepted NL0 and the fixed Lean interface.
4: They govern implementation, not additional NL0 detail or a weaker Audit B.
5: Use existing library readers and local checking tools; no separate review

9:    unfamiliar library application, establish its complete type in the pinned
10:    environment, including explicit, implicit and instance binders and all
11:    side conditions. Read the declaration or check a small typed application
12:    when its signature is uncertain. Do not infer the calling convention from
13:    its name or pass an implicit argument as though it were an explicit one.
14:    A previously checked signature in this context need not be looked up again.
15: 2. **Constrain difficult inference.** When coercions or implicit inference
16:    obscure the intended application, give the intermediate fact an explicit
17:    type and supply the relevant named parameters, such as the set, exponent
18:    or ambient space. Prefer this to leaving Lean to discover those choices by
19:    unfolding large definitions. Routine unambiguous arguments can stay
20:    implicit; explicit parameters must preserve the existing target and inputs.

22:    representations, first establish a small typed conversion fact, then use
23:    it in the main proof. In particular, distinguish `ℝ`, `ℝ≥0` and `ℝ≥0∞`;
24:    check the conversion direction, nonnegativity and any finiteness conditions.
25:    A conversion is not automatically invertible, and matching notation does
26:    not establish equality of differently typed expressions. Reuse a checked
27:    fact when available. Do not invent another representation, a global helper
28:    requirement or an extra hypothesis just to satisfy this instruction.
29: 4. **Isolate an inference failure.** If compiler feedback identifies a library
30:    application, coercion or expensive inference problem, reduce the next check
31:    to that application or conversion with explicit local types before adding
32:    more proof code. Use `check_auxiliary` in a proof worker, or
33:    `check_lean_types` during preparation when that tool is supplied. Helpers
34:    use only the current allowed inputs and never become new premises. Once
35:    the small check succeeds, integrate the result and recheck the complete
36:    obligation; success of a helper alone does not accept the target.

38: 5. **Repair after a bounded check.** Native checks have a separate per-call wall
39:    limit, normally 180 seconds, and use the controller-owned 20,000,000 heartbeat budget.
40:    A timeout or heartbeat diagnostic leaves the goal unaccepted and returns
41:    control to the same worker. Inspect the retained candidate and diagnostic,
42:    then check a smaller typed application, conversion or proof fragment before
43:    integrating it. Do not repeat the unchanged expensive candidate or disable
44:    limits to avoid diagnosis. Preserve the target, allowed inputs and proof
45:    requirements; a timeout alone establishes no mathematical gap.

A sphere-valued map cannot vanish outside a compact set. As approved by
the user on 2026-10-23, interpret spatial compact support as compact support
of a perturbation from a **fixed unit vector**, locally uniformly in time.
This is a disclosed nontrivial interpretation, not a claimed author-issued
correction.

Let \(n,m\geq1\) be integers and let
\(u:\mathbb R^n\times(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^m\) be jointly smooth.
Fix \(q\in\mathbb R^m\) with \(|q|=1\). Assume:

1. \(|u(x,t)|=1\) for all \(x\) and \(t>0\).
2. The acceleration \(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu\) is normal to the sphere at
   \(u\): at each point there is a real scalar \(a(x,t)\) with
   \(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu=a u\). No regularity of the selected scalar is
   assumed.
3. For every \(0<s<t<\infty\), a compact set
   \(C_{[s,t]}\subset\mathbb R^n\) exists such that \(u(x,r)=q\) for
   \(x\notin C_{[s,t]}\), \(r\in[s,t]\).

With Euclidean norms and Lebesgue measure, define

\[
e(x,t)=|u_t(x,t)|^2+\sum_{j=1}^n|\partial_{x_j}u(x,t)|^2,
\qquad E(t)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}e(x,t)\,dx.
\]

The spatial gradient square is the Frobenius square, and
\(\Delta_xu=\sum_j\partial_{x_jx_j}u\) component by component.
Prove integrability of \(e(\cdot,t)\), differentiability of \(E\),
and \(E'(t)=0\) for every \(t>0\). No assertion at time zero is required.

import Mathlib
open scoped BigOperators ContDiff Topology
open MeasureTheory
namespace WaveMap
abbrev Space (d : ℕ) := EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin d)
def timeDomain (n : ℕ) : Set (Space n × ℝ) := {p | 0 < p.2}
noncomputable def dt {n m : ℕ} (u : Space n → ℝ → Space m) (x : Space n) (t : ℝ) : Space m :=
  deriv (u x) t
noncomputable def dtt {n m : ℕ} (u : Space n → ℝ → Space m) (x : Space n) (t : ℝ) : Space m :=
  deriv (fun r => dt u x r) t
noncomputable def dx {n : ℕ} {F : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace ℝ F]
    (f : Space n → F) (j : Fin n) (x : Space n) : F :=
  fderiv ℝ f x (EuclideanSpace.single j 1)
noncomputable def du {n m : ℕ} (u : Space n → ℝ → Space m) (j : Fin n) (x : Space n) (t : ℝ) : Space m :=
  dx (fun y => u y t) j x
noncomputable def duu {n m : ℕ} (u : Space n → ℝ → Space m) (j : Fin n) (x : Space n) (t : ℝ) : Space m :=
  dx (fun y => du u j y t) j x
noncomputable def dut {n m : ℕ} (u : Space n → ℝ → Space m) (j : Fin n) (x : Space n) (t : ℝ) : Space m :=
  dx (fun y => dt u y t) j x
noncomputable def lap {n m : ℕ} (u : Space n → ℝ → Space m) (x : Space n) (t : ℝ) : Space m :=
  ∑ j, duu u j x t
noncomputable def density {n m : ℕ} (u : Space n → ℝ → Space m) (x : Space n) (t : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  ‖dt u x t‖ ^ 2 + ∑ j, ‖du u j x t‖ ^ 2
noncomputable def densityT {n m : ℕ} (u : Space n → ℝ → Space m) (x : Space n) (t : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  deriv (density u x) t
noncomputable def energy {n m : ℕ} (u : Space n → ℝ → Space m) (t : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  ∫ x, density u x t
noncomputable def flux {n m : ℕ} (u : Space n → ℝ → Space m) (j : Fin n) (t : ℝ) (x : Space n) : ℝ :=
  inner ℝ (dt u x t) (du u j x t)
def box {n : ℕ} (R : ℝ) : Set (Space n) := {x | ∀ j, x j ∈ Set.Icc (-R) R}
def openBox {n : ℕ} (R : ℝ) : Set (Space n) := {x | ∀ j, x j ∈ Set.Ioo (-R) R}
def sectionGood {n : ℕ} (f : Space n → ℝ) (C : Set (Space n)) (R : ℝ) : Prop :=
  Continuous f ∧ (∃ B : ℝ, ∀ x ∈ box (n := n) R, |f x| ≤ B) ∧
  (∀ x ∉ C, f x = 0) ∧ Integrable f
end WaveMap
